sections.h2: What does the Kansas homestead exemption actually cover?
sections.html:
In Kansas, people use the phrase homestead for three separate things: protection from forced sale by creditors, a yearly refund of part of the property tax, and a school-levy break on the first slice of a home's value. Only the first is a true exemption, and the other two work through different agencies.

The constitutional protection sits in Article 15, Section 9 of the Kansas Constitution and is repeated in K.S.A. 60-2301. It covers up to 160 acres of farm land, or one acre inside an incorporated town or city, or a manufactured or mobile home, occupied as a residence by the owner or the owner's family. Improvements on the land are included.

The tax refund is run by the Kansas Department of Revenue. The school-levy exemption comes from the state property tax statutes and is described by the Property Valuation Division. A seller who wants to know what a sale does to each of these has to look at them one at a time.

sections.h2: Can a creditor force the sale of a Kansas homestead?
sections.html:
Generally no, with a few written exceptions. The statute says a qualifying homestead is exempt from forced sale under any process of law, but no property is exempt from sale for taxes, or for debts contracted to buy the property or to build improvements on it.

The statute also says it does not apply to a lien given with the consent of both spouses, when the couple is married. That is why a mortgage can still be foreclosed even though the home is a homestead.

If a levy is made on land whose homestead has never been set apart, K.S.A. 60-2302 lets the householder, the spouse, or an agent or attorney give the officer a written notice describing what they regard as the homestead. That notice can come when the levy is made or at any time before the sale, and only the remainder can be sold.

For an owner behind on payments, the point is narrow. The exemption protects the home from forced sale in general, but the statute carves out taxes, purchase-money debts, improvement debts and liens both spouses consented to.

sections.h2: Does the homestead law change how a Kansas house is sold?
sections.html:
It can, when the owner is married. Section 60-2301 says a homestead cannot be alienated without the joint consent of husband and wife where that relation exists.

K.S.A. 60-2303 adds a rule about contracts. A suit for specific performance of a contract to sell a homestead, or for damages for breaking such a contract, cannot be maintained unless both spouses signed the contract, or an agent or broker authorized in writing by both did. The Kansas statute annotations note that this section does not apply to mortgages.

Practical steps for a married seller:

  • Have both spouses sign the sale contract, even if only one name is on the title.
  • If one spouse is not available, confirm with a Kansas attorney who can sign on their behalf.
  • Keep a written authorization if an agent will sign.

These rules protect the occupying family. They also mean a buyer will want to see both signatures before closing.

sections.h2: Who qualifies for the Kansas homestead property tax refund?
sections.html:
The K-40H refund is for people who own and occupy a Kansas home and lived in Kansas all of the tax year. The 2025 booklet from the Department of Revenue says renters do not qualify, and that a name on the deed or a contract for deed counts as ownership while a rent-to-own contract does not.

A household with total income of $43,389 or less qualifies if at least one of these is true:

  • The claimant was born before January 1, 1970.
  • The claimant was blind, totally and permanently disabled, or a disabled veteran for all of 2025.
  • A dependent child under 18 lived with the claimant all year.

Only one claim can be filed per household. Household income counts most taxable and nontaxable income, but only half of Social Security and SSI benefits on the K-40H, and Social Security disability payments are left out.

sections.h2: How is the refund calculated and when is it paid?
sections.html:
The refund is a percentage of the general property tax paid, with a ceiling on the tax counted. The refund percentage depends on income: 100 percent at $6,000 or less, 50 percent for incomes from $17,001 to $18,000, 10 percent for $25,001 to $26,000, and 5 percent for incomes from $26,001 up to the $43,389 limit. Income of $43,390 or more gets nothing.

The tax counted is the lower of the tax billed or $700, and taxes on property valued at more than $350,000 do not qualify. Special assessments, service charges and late interest are left out. A refund under $5 is not paid.

Two property tax installments are in play. The 2025 tax was due in two parts, December 20, 2025 and May 10, 2026, and the K-40H counts both whether or not they have been paid. Paper claims that are complete take about 20 to 24 weeks to process.

If the home carries delinquent property tax, the Department of Revenue sends the whole refund to the county treasurer. A refund can also be taken for other debts owed to the state.

Late claims can be accepted for good cause if filed within four years of the original due date. The department also offers an optional Refund Advancement Program that applies part of an expected refund to the first-half tax bill.

sections.h2: What happens to the refund when a home is sold or the owner dies?
sections.html:
The booklet says a homeowner who moved during the year can claim the general property tax paid for the time lived in each residence. A homeowner who rented out part of the house can claim only the tax on the part they lived in, worked out by the share of rooms rented or used for business.

For an owner who has died, another qualifying member of the household files the claim for the household. If no household member qualifies, a claim can be filed for the deceased claimant when they lived in Kansas for the part of the year they were alive. The refund is prorated by the month of death, from 8.3 percent for January up to 100 percent for December. The claim needs a death certificate, funeral home notice or obituary, plus letters of administration if the estate is in probate or Form RF-9 if it is not.

Heirs who inherit a Kansas house often find the property tax bill, not the refund, is the first deadline. The Department of Revenue's sales validation form treats estimated real estate taxes prorated for the year of sale as a normal escrow closing cost, so the split between seller and buyer is usually settled at closing.

sections.h2: What is the $75,000 school levy exemption?
sections.html:
For tax year 2024 and every year after, the first $75,000 of appraised value of residential property is exempt from the statewide school finance levy. The Property Valuation Division notice describes it as limited to the 20 mill school district levy.

The division's legislative summary ties the figure to Senate Bill 1 from the 2024 special session. That bill stopped the earlier formula that raised the amount each year by the average statewide increase in value.

faqs.q: Is the Kansas homestead exemption the same as the homestead refund?
faqs.a: No. The exemption in Article 15, Section 9 and K.S.A. 60-2301 protects a home from forced sale. The K-40H refund is a partial property tax rebate that the Department of Revenue pays on a claim.

faqs.q: How much is the Kansas homestead refund?
faqs.a: The maximum for 2025 was $700, calculated as a percentage of general property tax based on household income. Taxes on property valued above $350,000 do not qualify.

faqs.q: When do I file a Kansas homestead claim?
faqs.a: For 2025, after December 31, 2025 and no later than April 15, 2026. Late claims can be accepted for good cause within four years of the original due date.

faqs.q: Do both spouses have to sign to sell a Kansas homestead?
faqs.a: Under K.S.A. 60-2301 and 60-2303, a homestead cannot be alienated without the joint consent of the spouses, and a suit to enforce a sale contract needs the signature of both or of an agent they authorized in writing.

faqs.q: Can I get the homestead refund if I rent out part of my house?
faqs.a: Yes, but only for the part you live in. The booklet uses a room-count worksheet, and rental income is reported on the claim.
